title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Extraordinary Restraints on Importing Almost Every Kind of Goods from Countries with Which the Balance of Trade Is Thought to Be Unfavourable
Part I — Why These Restraints Are Unreasonable, Even on the Principles of the Commercial System

The commercial system's second device for increasing a country's stock of gold and silver is to impose unusually heavy restrictions on importing nearly every kind of good from the particular countries with which the balance of trade is thought to run against us. In Great Britain, for instance, Silesian lawns can be imported for home use if certain duties are paid, but French cambrics and lawns may not be imported at all except into the port of London, and then only to be warehoused for re-export. French wines are taxed more heavily than Portuguese wines, or indeed than the wines of any other country. The measure known as the impost of 1692 placed a duty of twenty-five per cent of the assessed value on all French goods, whereas goods from other nations were mostly charged far lighter duties, rarely above five per cent. French wine, brandy, salt, and vinegar were exempted from this particular tax, but only because other laws, or special clauses within the same law, already loaded them with heavy duties of their own. In 1696, since the first duty had not seemed discouraging enough, a second duty of twenty-five per cent was laid on all French goods except brandy, along with a new duty of twenty-five pounds on every ton of French wine and another fifteen pounds on every ton of French vinegar. French goods have never been left out of any of those general five-per-cent subsidies or duties imposed on all, or nearly all, of the goods listed in the book of rates. If we treat the one-third and two-third subsidies together as making up one complete subsidy, there have been five such general subsidies in all. So, before the present war began, seventy-five per cent could be regarded as the lowest duty to which most goods grown, produced, or manufactured in France were liable. On most goods, duties of that size amount to an outright ban. The French, for their part, have, I believe, treated our goods and manufactures just as harshly, though I am less familiar with the specific burdens they have placed on them. These mutual restraints have killed off almost all honest trade between the two nations, and smugglers are now the chief importers of British goods into France and of French goods into Britain. The arguments I examined in the previous chapter grew out of private interest and the spirit of monopoly; those I am about to examine here grow out of national prejudice and hostility. They are therefore, as you might expect, even more unreasonable — and unreasonable even by the standards of the commercial system itself.

First, suppose it were certain that in a free trade between France and England the balance would favour France. It would still not follow that such trade would harm England, or that the overall balance of England's whole trade would be tipped further against it. If French wines are better and cheaper than Portuguese ones, or French linens better and cheaper than German ones, then Britain would be better off buying both the wine and the foreign linen it needs from France rather than from Portugal and Germany. The total value of what Britain imported each year from France would rise sharply, yet the total value of all its annual imports would fall, by exactly as much as the equally good French goods cost less than those of the other two countries. This would hold true even if every French good imported were consumed entirely within Britain.

But, second, a large share of those French goods could be re-exported to other countries, sold there at a profit, and bring back a return worth perhaps as much as the original cost of all the French goods imported. What has often been said of the East India trade might well be true of the French trade too: that although most East India goods were bought with gold and silver, re-exporting some of them to other countries brought back more gold and silver to the nation carrying on the trade than the whole original purchase had cost. One of the most important branches of Dutch trade today consists in carrying French goods to other European countries. Even some of the French wine drunk in Britain is smuggled in by way of Holland and Zealand. If there were either free trade between France and England, or if French goods could be imported on paying only the same duties as goods from other European nations — duties refundable on re-export — England might claim a share of a trade that has proved so profitable for Holland.

Third and last, there is no reliable test by which we can decide which way the so-called balance lies between any two countries, or which of them exports the greater value. National prejudice and hostility, always egged on by the private interest of particular traders, are what usually steer our judgment on every question of this kind. Two tests, however, have often been invoked on such occasions: the custom-house books and the rate of exchange. The custom-house books, it is now generally admitted, are a very unreliable test, because most goods are valued in them so inaccurately. The rate of exchange is perhaps almost as unreliable.

When the exchange between two places — say London and Paris — stands at par, this is said to show that the debts owed by London to Paris are matched by those owed by Paris to London. When, by contrast, a premium has to be paid in London for a bill drawn on Paris, this is said to show that London's debts to Paris are not matched by Paris's debts to London, so that a balance of money must be sent from London to Paris; and the premium is asked and paid to cover the risk, trouble, and expense of shipping that money. But the usual state of debt and credit between two cities, the argument runs, must be governed by the usual course of their dealings with each other. When neither imports from the other more than it exports to it, the debts and credits on each side can cancel out. But when one of them imports from the other more than it exports to it, that one necessarily ends up owing more than it is owed; the debts and credits no longer cancel, and money must be sent from the place whose debts outweigh its credits. So the usual rate of exchange, being a sign of the usual state of debt and credit between two places, must also be a sign of the usual course of their exports and imports, since these are what govern that state.

But even granting that the usual rate of exchange does reliably indicate the usual state of debt and credit between two places, it still would not follow that the balance of trade favoured whichever place had the state of debt and credit in its favour. The usual state of debt and credit between two places is not always governed entirely by their dealings with each other; it is often shaped by either one's dealings with many other places besides. Suppose, for example, that English merchants usually pay for goods they buy from Hamburg, Danzig, Riga, and so on by means of bills drawn on Holland. Then the usual state of debt and credit between England and Holland will not be governed solely by the two countries' direct dealings, but will be affected by England's dealings with all those other places. England might have to send money to Holland every year even though its yearly exports to Holland far exceed the value of its imports from there, and even though the so-called balance of trade is heavily in England's favour.

What is more, given the way the par of exchange has been calculated up to now, the usual rate of exchange can give no reliable sign that the usual state of debt and credit favours the country that appears to have, or is supposed to have, the usual rate of exchange in its favour. In other words, the real exchange may be — and in fact often is — so different from the calculated exchange that, on many occasions, no firm conclusion about the real exchange can be drawn from the calculated one.

When you pay a sum of money in England containing, by the standard of the English mint, a certain number of ounces of pure silver, and in return receive a bill for a sum payable in France containing, by the standard of the French mint, an equal number of ounces of pure silver, the exchange is said to be at par between England and France. When you have to pay more, you are taken to be paying a premium, and the exchange is said to be against England and in favour of France. When you pay less, you are taken to be getting a premium, and the exchange is said to be against France and in favour of England.

But, first, we cannot always judge the value of one country's currency against another's by the standards of their respective mints. In some countries the coin is more worn, clipped, or otherwise degraded below its standard than in others. The value of any country's coin, compared with that of any other, depends not on how much pure silver it ought to contain but on how much it actually does contain. Before the silver coinage was reformed in King William's reign, the exchange between England and Holland, reckoned in the usual way by the standards of their respective mints, ran twenty-five per cent against England. But the actual English coin, as Mr Lowndes tells us, was at that time rather more than twenty-five per cent below its standard value. So the real exchange may even then have favoured England, despite the calculated exchange running so heavily against it: a smaller number of ounces of pure silver actually paid in England may have bought a bill for a larger number of ounces payable in Holland, and the man supposedly paying the premium may in reality have been the one receiving it. Before the recent reform of the English gold coin, the French coin was far less worn than the English and was perhaps two or three per cent nearer its standard. So if the calculated exchange with France ran no more than two or three per cent against England, the real exchange might actually have been in England's favour. Since the reform of the gold coin, the exchange has been steadily in England's favour and against France.

Second, in some countries the cost of coinage is borne by the government, while in others it is borne by private people who bring their bullion to the mint, and the government even draws some revenue from the coinage. In England the government bears the cost: bring a pound weight of standard silver to the mint and you get back sixty-two shillings, containing a pound weight of silver of the same standard. In France, a duty of eight per cent is deducted to cover the coinage, which not only pays for the work but yields a small revenue to the government. In England, since coinage costs nothing, the coin can never be worth much more than the bullion it actually contains. In France, the workmanship — which you have paid for — adds to the value, just as it does with wrought silver plate. So a sum of French money containing a given weight of pure silver is worth more than a sum of English money containing the same weight, and requires more bullion or other goods to buy it. Even if the coin of the two countries were equally close to the standards of their mints, a sum of English money could not really buy a sum of French money containing the same number of ounces of pure silver — and therefore could not buy a bill on France for such a sum either. If, for such a bill, no more extra money were paid than enough to make up for the cost of French coinage, the real exchange might stand at par between the two countries, their debts and credits cancelling out, even while the calculated exchange ran considerably in France's favour. And if less than that were paid, the real exchange might actually favour England while the calculated one favoured France.

Third and last, in some places — Amsterdam, Hamburg, Venice, and so on — foreign bills of exchange are paid in what is called bank money, while in others — London, Lisbon, Antwerp, Leghorn, and so on — they are paid in the country's ordinary currency. Bank money is always worth more than the same nominal sum of ordinary currency. A thousand guilders in the bank of Amsterdam, for instance, are worth more than a thousand guilders of Amsterdam currency. The difference between them is called the bank's agio, which at Amsterdam is generally about five per cent. Suppose the coin of two countries is equally close to the standards of their respective mints, but that one pays foreign bills in ordinary currency while the other pays them in bank money. Then clearly the calculated exchange may favour the one paying in bank money even though the real exchange favours the one paying in ordinary currency — for the same reason that the calculated exchange may favour the country paying in better money, or money nearer its own standard, even when the real exchange favours the country paying in worse. Before the recent reform of the gold coin, the calculated exchange generally ran against London with Amsterdam, Hamburg, Venice, and, I believe, every other place that pays in bank money. It does not follow, however, that the real exchange ran against London. Since the reform of the gold coin, the exchange has favoured London even with those places. The calculated exchange has generally favoured London with Lisbon, Antwerp, Leghorn, and — France excepted — I believe with most other parts of Europe that pay in ordinary currency; and it is quite likely that the real exchange favoured London too.
A Digression on Banks of Deposit, and Particularly on the Bank of Amsterdam

The currency of a large state, such as France or England, generally consists almost entirely of its own coin. So if that currency ever becomes worn, clipped, or otherwise degraded below its standard value, the state can effectively restore it by reforming the coinage. But the currency of a small state, such as Genoa or Hamburg, can rarely consist wholly of its own coin; it is largely made up of the coins of all the neighbouring states with which its people are in constant contact. Such a state, therefore, cannot always reform its currency simply by reforming its own coin. If foreign bills of exchange are paid in this mixed currency, the uncertain value of any sum of something so inherently uncertain must make the exchange always run heavily against such a state, since its currency is bound to be valued in every foreign country even below what it is actually worth.

To remedy the disadvantage this poor exchange must have caused their merchants, such small states, once they began to look after the interests of trade, often decreed that foreign bills of exchange above a certain value should be paid not in ordinary currency but by an order drawn on, or a transfer in the books of, a particular bank set up on the credit and under the protection of the state — a bank always bound to pay in good, genuine money exactly according to the state's standard. The banks of Venice, Genoa, Amsterdam, Hamburg, and Nuremberg all seem to have been originally founded with this purpose, though some were later put to other uses as well. The money of such banks, being better than the country's ordinary currency, necessarily commanded an agio, larger or smaller according to how far the currency was thought to be degraded below the state's standard. The agio of the bank of Hamburg, for instance — said to run commonly about fourteen per cent — is the supposed difference between the state's good standard money and the clipped, worn, and diminished currency poured into the country from all the neighbouring states.

Before 1609, the huge quantity of clipped and worn foreign coin that Amsterdam's vast trade drew in from all over Europe had reduced the value of its currency about nine per cent below that of good money fresh from the mint. As soon as such good money appeared, it was melted down or carried off, as always happens in such circumstances. Merchants, awash in currency, could not always find enough good money to settle their bills of exchange; and the value of those bills, despite several regulations meant to prevent it, became largely uncertain.

To cure these troubles, a bank was set up in 1609 under the guarantee of the city. It took in both foreign coin and the light, worn coin of the country at its real intrinsic value in the country's good standard money, deducting only enough to cover the cost of coinage and the other necessary expenses of management. For the value left after that small deduction, it granted a credit in its books. This credit was called bank money, and because it represented money exactly according to the mint standard, it always held the same real value and was intrinsically worth more than the currency in circulation. At the same time it was enacted that all bills drawn on or negotiated at Amsterdam worth 600 guilders or more must be paid in bank money, which at a stroke removed all uncertainty about the value of such bills. As a result, every merchant had to keep an account with the bank in order to pay his foreign bills of exchange, and this necessarily created a steady demand for bank money.

Bank money, besides being intrinsically better than currency and gaining still more value from this demand, also has other advantages. It is safe from fire, robbery, and other accidents; the city of Amsterdam stands surety for it; and it can be paid away by a simple transfer, with no need to count it out and no risk in carrying it from place to place. Because of these advantages, it seems to have commanded an agio from the start; and it is generally believed that all the money first deposited in the bank was left there, nobody caring to claim payment on a debt he could sell at a premium in the market. By claiming payment from the bank, the owner of a bank credit would lose that premium. Just as a shilling fresh from the mint buys no more goods in the market than one of our common worn shillings, so the good, true money that might be drawn from the bank's vaults into a private person's coffers, once mixed and merged with the country's ordinary currency, would be worth no more than that currency, since it could no longer be readily told apart from it. As long as it stayed in the bank's vaults, its superiority was known and certain. Once in a private person's hands, its superiority could not easily be established without more trouble than the difference was perhaps worth. Drawn from the bank's vaults, besides, it lost all the other advantages of bank money — its security, its easy and safe transfer, its usefulness in paying foreign bills of exchange. On top of all this, as will become clear shortly, it could not be drawn from those vaults without first paying for its keeping.

These deposits of coin — or deposits the bank was bound to repay in coin — made up the bank's original capital, the whole value represented by what is called bank money. Today they are thought to make up only a very small part of it. To make the bullion trade easier, the bank has for many years past granted credit in its books on deposits of gold and silver bullion. This credit is generally about five per cent below the mint price of such bullion. At the same time the bank grants what is called a recipisse, or receipt, entitling the depositor or the bearer to take out the bullion again at any time within six months, on transferring back to the bank an amount of bank money equal to the credit granted when the deposit was made, and on paying one-quarter per cent for the keeping if the deposit was silver, or one-half per cent if it was gold. But the bank also declares that if this payment is not made and the term expires, the deposit shall belong to the bank at the price at which it was received, or for which credit was given in the transfer books. What is thus paid for keeping the deposit may be regarded as a kind of warehouse rent; and several reasons have been offered for why this rent should be so much higher for gold than for silver. The fineness of gold, it is said, is harder to determine than that of silver. Frauds are more easily worked, and cause a greater loss, in the more precious metal. Besides, since silver is the standard metal, the state is said to wish to encourage deposits of silver more than deposits of gold.

Bullion is most often deposited when its price is somewhat lower than usual, and taken out again when the price happens to rise. In Holland the market price of bullion generally stands above the mint price, for the same reason it did in England before the recent reform of the gold coin. The difference is said to run commonly from about six to sixteen stivers on the mark — eight ounces of silver, eleven parts fine to one part alloy. The bank price, or the credit the bank gives for deposits of such silver (when made in foreign coin of well-known and certain fineness, such as Mexico dollars), is twenty-two guilders the mark; the mint price is about twenty-three guilders; and the market price runs from twenty-three guilders six stivers to twenty-three guilders sixteen stivers, or from two to three per cent above the mint price.
The following are the prices at which the bank of Amsterdam at present {September 1775} receives bullion and coin of various kinds:

SILVER — Mexico dollars ................. 22 Guilders / mark; French crowns .................. 22; English silver coin ............. 22; Mexico dollars, new coin ........ 21 10; Ducatoons ....................... 3 0; Rix-dollars ..................... 2 8
Bar silver containing eleven-twelfths fine silver, 21 Guilders / mark, and in this proportion down to one-quarter fine, on which 5 guilders are given. Fine bars ................. 28 Guilders / mark.

Bar or ingot gold is received in proportion to its fineness, judged against the foreign gold coin listed above. On fine bars the bank gives 340 per mark. In general, though, something more is given for coin of known fineness than for gold and silver bars, whose fineness can be determined only by melting and assaying.

The ratios between the bank price, the mint price, and the market price of gold bullion are nearly the same. A person can generally sell his receipt for the difference between the mint price of bullion and the market price. A receipt for bullion is almost always worth something, so it very rarely happens that anyone lets his receipts lapse, or lets his bullion fall to the bank at the price at which it was received — either by failing to take it out before the six months are up, or by neglecting to pay the one-quarter or one-half per cent needed to obtain a fresh receipt for another six months. This does happen sometimes, however rarely, and more often with gold than with silver, because of the higher warehouse rent paid for keeping the more precious metal.

A man who deposits bullion gets both a bank credit and a receipt. He pays his bills of exchange as they fall due with his bank credit, and either sells or holds his receipt depending on whether he expects the price of bullion to rise or fall. The receipt and the bank credit rarely stay long in the same hands, and there is no need for them to. A man who holds a receipt and wants to draw out bullion can always find plenty of bank credits, or bank money, to buy at the going price; and a man who holds bank money and wants to draw out bullion can always find receipts in equal abundance.

The owners of bank credits and the holders of receipts form two distinct kinds of creditors against the bank. The holder of a receipt cannot draw out the bullion it covers without handing back to the bank a sum of bank money equal to the price at which the bullion was received. If he has no bank money of his own, he must buy it from those who do. The owner of bank money cannot draw out bullion without presenting to the bank receipts for the amount he wants. If he has none of his own, he must buy them from those who do. When the holder of a receipt buys bank money, he is buying the power to take out a quantity of bullion whose mint price is five per cent above the bank price. So the five-per-cent agio he commonly pays for it is paid not for an imaginary value but for a real one. When the owner of bank money buys a receipt, he is buying the power to take out a quantity of bullion whose market price is commonly two or three per cent above the mint price. So what he pays for it is likewise paid for a real value. The price of the receipt and the price of the bank money together make up the full value or price of the bullion.

On deposits of the country's ordinary coin, the bank grants receipts as well as bank credits, but these receipts are often worthless and will fetch no price in the market. On ducatoons, for example, which pass in the currency for three guilders three stivers each, the bank gives a credit of only three guilders, or five per cent below their current value. It also grants a receipt entitling the bearer to take out the number of ducatoons deposited at any time within six months, on paying one-quarter per cent for the keeping. This receipt will often fetch no price in the market. Three guilders of bank money generally sell in the market for three guilders three stivers — the full value of the ducatoons if they were taken out of the bank; and before they can be taken out, one-quarter per cent must be paid for the keeping, which would be pure loss to the holder of the receipt. If the bank's agio should ever fall to three per cent, such receipts might fetch some price and sell for one and three-quarters per cent. But since the agio now generally runs about five per cent, such receipts are often left to lapse, or, as they say, to fall to the bank. The receipts given for deposits of gold ducats fall to it still more often, because a higher warehouse rent — one-half per cent — must be paid for keeping them before they can be taken out again. The five per cent the bank gains when deposits of either coin or bullion are allowed to fall to it may be regarded as the warehouse rent for keeping such deposits permanently.

The sum of bank money whose receipts have lapsed must be very large. It must include the bank's whole original capital, which is generally supposed to have stayed there ever since it was first deposited, nobody caring either to renew his receipt or to take out his deposit, since, for the reasons already given, neither could be done without loss. But whatever the size of this sum, the share it forms of the whole mass of bank money is thought to be very small. For many years past the bank of Amsterdam has been Europe's great warehouse for bullion, whose receipts are very rarely allowed to lapse, or, as they say, to fall to the bank. By far the greater part of the bank money — that is, of the credits on the bank's books — is supposed to have been created over these many years by such bullion deposits, which the dealers in bullion are constantly both making and withdrawing.

No claim can be made on the bank except by means of a recipisse, or receipt. The smaller mass of bank money whose receipts have lapsed is mixed and merged with the much larger mass whose receipts are still in force; so although there may be a considerable sum of bank money for which no receipts exist, there is no specific sum or portion of it that could not, at any moment, be claimed by some receipt-holder. The bank cannot owe the same thing to two people; and the owner of bank money who holds no receipt cannot claim payment from the bank until he buys one. In ordinary, quiet times he has no trouble finding one to buy at the market price, which generally matches the price at which he can sell the coin or bullion the receipt entitles him to take out of the bank.

It might be otherwise during a public disaster — an invasion, for instance, like that of the French in 1672. With the owners of bank money all scrambling to draw it out and keep it in their own hands, the demand for receipts could drive their price to an outrageous height. The holders of receipts might form wild expectations and, instead of two or three per cent, demand half the bank money credited on the deposits their receipts had been granted for. The enemy, knowing how the bank was set up, might even buy the receipts up in order to stop the treasure from being carried away. In such emergencies the bank, it is supposed, would set aside its ordinary rule of paying only the holders of receipts. The receipt-holders who held no bank money would have received within two or three per cent of the value of the deposit their respective receipts were granted for. So the bank, it is said, would in this case not hesitate to pay, in money or bullion, the full value credited in its books to the owners of bank money who could get no receipts — while paying two or three per cent to those receipt-holders who held no bank money, that being the whole value justly supposed due to them in such circumstances.

Even in ordinary, quiet times it is in the interest of receipt-holders to push the agio down, so as either to buy bank money — and therefore the bullion their receipts would then let them take out of the bank — that much cheaper, or to sell their receipts to those who hold bank money and want to take out bullion that much dearer; for the price of a receipt is generally equal to the difference between the market price of bank money and the market price of the coin or bullion the receipt was granted for. The owners of bank money, by contrast, have an interest in pushing the agio up, so as either to sell their bank money that much dearer or to buy a receipt that much cheaper. To check the stock-jobbing tricks that these opposing interests might sometimes produce, the bank has in recent years resolved to sell bank money for currency at all times at a five-per-cent agio, and to buy it back at a four-per-cent agio. As a result, the agio can never rise above five or sink below four per cent, and the ratio between the market price of bank money and that of currency is kept at all times very close to the ratio between their intrinsic values. Before this resolution, the market price of bank money used sometimes to rise as high as a nine-per-cent agio and sometimes to sink as low as par, according to how the opposing interests happened to sway the market.

The bank of Amsterdam claims to lend out no part of what is deposited with it, but for every guilder it credits in its books to keep in its vaults the value of a guilder in either money or bullion. That it keeps in its vaults all the money or bullion covered by receipts still in force — which it may be called upon to pay at any time, and which in reality is constantly leaving it and returning again — can hardly be doubted. But whether it does the same with the part of its capital whose receipts lapsed long ago — which in ordinary, quiet times it cannot be called upon to pay, and which in reality is very likely to stay with it forever, or as long as the United Provinces last — may seem more doubtful. At Amsterdam, however, no article of faith is more firmly held than that for every guilder circulating as bank money there is a matching guilder in gold or silver to be found in the bank's treasury. The city guarantees that it is so. The bank is run by the four reigning burgomasters, who change every year. Each new set of burgomasters inspects the treasure, compares it with the books, receives it upon oath, and hands it over with the same solemn ceremony to the set that follows; and in that sober, religious country, oaths are not yet treated lightly. A rotation of this kind seems by itself a sufficient safeguard against any practices that could not be openly admitted. Through all the upheavals that faction has ever caused in the government of Amsterdam, the party in power has never once accused its predecessors of dishonesty in running the bank. No charge could have damaged the reputation and fortune of a disgraced party more deeply, and we may be sure that if such a charge could have been made good, it would have been brought. In 1672, when the French king was at Utrecht, the bank of Amsterdam paid out so readily as to leave no doubt of the fidelity with which it had kept its engagements. Some of the coins then brought out of its vaults appeared to have been scorched by the fire that broke out in the town hall soon after the bank was founded. Those coins, then, must have lain there ever since.

How great the bank's treasure may be is a question that has long exercised the speculations of the curious. Nothing but guesswork can be offered about it. It is generally reckoned that about 2,000 people keep accounts with the bank; and allowing each, on average, to hold the value of £1,500 sterling on his account — a very generous allowance — the whole quantity of bank money, and therefore of treasure in the bank, would come to about £3,000,000 sterling, or, at eleven guilders to the pound sterling, 33,000,000 guilders: a great sum, enough to carry on a very extensive circulation, but far below the extravagant notions some people have formed of this treasure.

The city of Amsterdam draws a considerable revenue from the bank. Besides the warehouse rent already mentioned, each person pays a fee of ten guilders on first opening an account; three guilders three stivers for every new account; two stivers for every transfer; and, if the transfer is for less than 300 guilders, six stivers, in order to discourage a multitude of small transactions. Anyone who fails to balance his account twice a year forfeits twenty-five guilders. Anyone who orders a transfer for more than stands on his account must pay three per cent on the amount overdrawn, and his order is set aside besides. The bank is also supposed to make a considerable profit by selling the foreign coin or bullion that sometimes falls to it when receipts lapse, which is always held until it can be sold at a profit. It profits, too, by selling bank money at a five-per-cent agio and buying it back at four. These various sources of income come to a good deal more than is needed to pay the officers' salaries and cover the cost of management. What is paid for keeping bullion on receipts is alone supposed to yield a clear annual revenue of between 150,000 and 200,000 guilders. The original aim of the institution, however, was public utility, not revenue. Its purpose was to relieve merchants of the inconvenience of an unfavourable exchange. The revenue that has arisen from it was unforeseen and may be regarded as incidental. But it is now time to return from this long digression, into which I have been led almost without noticing, in trying to explain why the exchange between countries that pay in bank money and those that pay in ordinary currency should generally appear to favour the former and run against the latter. The former pay in a kind of money whose intrinsic value is always the same and exactly matches the standard of their respective mints; the latter pay in a kind of money whose intrinsic value is constantly shifting and is almost always more or less below that standard.
Part II — Why These Extraordinary Restraints Are Unreasonable on Other Grounds

In the earlier part of this chapter I have tried to show, even on the principles of the commercial system, how needless it is to lay extraordinary restraints on importing goods from those countries with which the balance of trade is thought to run against us.

Nothing, however, could be more absurd than the whole doctrine of the balance of trade, on which not only these restraints but almost every other regulation of commerce is founded. When two places trade with each other, this doctrine assumes that if the balance is even, neither loses or gains; but that if it tilts at all to one side, one of them loses and the other gains, in proportion to how far it departs from exact equilibrium. Both assumptions are false. Trade forced into being by bounties and monopolies may be, and commonly is, disadvantageous to the very country it is meant to favour, as I shall try to show later. But trade that is carried on naturally and regularly between two places, without force or constraint, is always advantageous to both, though not always equally so.

By advantage or gain I do not mean an increase in the quantity of gold and silver, but an increase in the exchangeable value of the annual produce of a country's land and labour — that is, an increase in the annual income of its people.

If the balance is even, and the trade between two places consists entirely in exchanging their native goods, then in most cases both will not only gain but gain equally, or very nearly so. Each, in this case, provides a market for part of the other's surplus produce; each replaces a capital that had been employed in raising and preparing for market that part of the other's surplus produce, and that had been spread among, and given income and livelihood to, a certain number of the other's people. So some of each country's people will draw their income and livelihood directly from the other. And since the goods exchanged are assumed to be of equal value, the two capitals employed in the trade will in most cases be equal, or very nearly so; and since both are employed in raising the native goods of the two countries, the income and livelihood their distribution provides to the people of each will be equal, or very nearly equal. This income and livelihood, thus furnished to each other, will be greater or smaller in proportion to the size of their dealings. If these came each year, say, to £100,000 or to £1,000,000 on each side, then each would furnish the other's people with an annual income of £100,000 in the one case, and of £1,000,000 in the other.

Suppose instead their trade were such that one of them exported nothing but native goods, while the returns from the other consisted entirely of foreign goods. The balance would still be reckoned even, since goods are paid for with goods. In this case too both would gain, but they would not gain equally; and the people of the country that exported nothing but native goods would draw the greater income from the trade. If England, for example, imported from France nothing but French native goods, and — having no goods of its own that were in demand there — repaid them each year by sending over a large quantity of foreign goods, say tobacco and East India goods, this trade, though it would give some income to the people of both countries, would give more to those of France than to those of England. The whole French capital employed in it each year would be distributed among the people of France; but only that part of the English capital used to produce the English goods with which those foreign goods were bought would be distributed each year among the people of England. The greater part of it would replace the capitals that had been employed in Virginia, Hindustan, and China, and that had given income and livelihood to the people of those distant countries. So if the capitals were equal, or nearly equal, this employment of the French capital would increase the income of the French people far more than the English capital would increase that of the English. France, in this case, would be carrying on a direct foreign trade of consumption with England, while England would be carrying on a roundabout trade of the same kind with France. The different effects of a capital employed in the direct, and of one employed in the roundabout, foreign trade of consumption have already been fully explained.

There is probably no trade between any two countries that consists entirely either in the exchange of native goods on both sides, or of native goods on one side and foreign goods on the other. Almost all countries exchange with one another a mix of native and foreign goods. But the country whose cargoes carry the largest proportion of native, and the smallest of foreign, goods will always be the chief gainer.

Suppose England paid for the goods it imported each year from France not with tobacco and East India goods but with gold and silver. The balance would then be reckoned uneven, since goods would be paid for not with goods but with gold and silver. Yet the trade would, as before, give some income to the people of both countries, though more to those of France than to those of England. It would give some income to England's people. The capital used to produce the English goods that bought this gold and silver — the capital that had been distributed among, and given income to, certain people in England — would thereby be replaced and enabled to carry on the same employment. England's whole capital would be no more reduced by this export of gold and silver than by the export of an equal value of any other goods. On the contrary, in most cases it would be increased. No goods are sent abroad except those for which the demand is supposed greater abroad than at home, and whose returns are therefore expected to be worth more at home than the goods exported. If tobacco worth only £100,000 in England, sent to France, will buy wine worth £110,000 in England, the exchange will increase England's capital by £10,000. And if £100,000 of English gold, in the same way, buys French wine worth £110,000 in England, this exchange will likewise increase England's capital by £10,000. Just as a merchant with £110,000 worth of wine in his cellar is a richer man than one with only £100,000 worth of tobacco in his warehouse, so he is likewise richer than one with only £100,000 worth of gold in his coffers. He can set a greater quantity of industry in motion, and give income, livelihood, and employment to a greater number of people, than either of the other two. But a country's capital is equal to the combined capital of all its people, and the quantity of industry it can keep going each year is equal to what all those separate capitals together can maintain. So both the country's capital and the quantity of industry it can maintain each year must generally be increased by this exchange. It would, indeed, be more advantageous for England to be able to buy French wines with its own hardware and broadcloth than with either the tobacco of Virginia or the gold and silver of Brazil and Peru. A direct foreign trade of consumption is always more advantageous than a roundabout one. But a roundabout foreign trade of consumption carried on with gold and silver does not seem any less advantageous than any other equally roundabout one. Nor is a country with no mines any more likely to be drained of gold and silver by this yearly export of those metals than one which grows no tobacco is to be drained of tobacco by the like yearly export of that plant. Just as a country with the means to buy tobacco will never be long without it, so a country with the means to buy gold and silver will never be long without those metals.

It is a losing trade, people say, that a workman carries on with the alehouse; and the trade a manufacturing nation would naturally carry on with a wine-producing country may be thought of as the same sort of thing. My answer is that the trade with the alehouse is not necessarily a losing one. In its own nature it is just as advantageous as any other, though perhaps somewhat more open to abuse. The work of a brewer, and even of a retailer of fermented liquors, are as necessary a division of labour as any other. It will generally be more advantageous for a workman to buy the quantity he needs from the brewer than to brew it himself; and if he is a poor workman, it will generally be more advantageous for him to buy it little by little from the retailer than in a large quantity from the brewer. He may of course buy too much of either, just as he may from any other dealer in his neighbourhood — from the butcher if he is a glutton, or from the draper if he likes to play the fine gentleman among his friends. Yet it is to the advantage of the great body of workmen that all these trades should be free, even though that freedom may be abused in every one of them, and is perhaps more likely to be abused in some than in others. And though individuals may sometimes ruin their fortunes by drinking too much fermented liquor, there seems to be no danger that a nation will do so. In every country there are many people who spend more on such liquors than they can afford, but there are always many more who spend less. It is worth noting, too, that experience suggests cheap wine is a cause not of drunkenness but of sobriety. The people of the wine-producing countries are generally the soberest in Europe — witness the Spaniards, the Italians, and the people of the southern provinces of France. People are seldom guilty of excess in what is their daily fare. Nobody plays the generous good fellow by being lavish with a liquor as cheap as small beer. On the contrary, in the countries that, from excessive heat or cold, grow no grapes — so that wine is dear and rare — drunkenness is a common vice, as among the northern nations and all those who live between the tropics, the Negroes on the coast of Guinea, for example. When a French regiment comes from one of the northern provinces of France, where wine is somewhat dear, to be quartered in the south, where it is very cheap, the soldiers, I have often heard it observed, are at first led astray by the cheapness and novelty of good wine; but after a few months' residence most of them become as sober as the rest of the inhabitants. If the duties on foreign wines and the excises on malt, beer, and ale were all swept away at once, it might in the same way bring on a fairly general but temporary drunkenness in Britain among the middling and lower ranks, which would probably soon be followed by a lasting and almost universal sobriety. At present drunkenness is by no means the vice of fashionable people, or of those who can easily afford the most expensive liquors. A gentleman drunk on ale has hardly ever been seen among us. The restraints on the wine trade in Britain, besides, seem designed not so much to keep people from going, so to speak, to the alehouse, as to keep them from going where they can buy the best and cheapest liquor. They favour the wine trade of Portugal and discourage that of France. The Portuguese, it is said, are better customers for our manufactures than the French, and so should be favoured over them. Since they give us their custom, the pretence runs, we should give them ours. The sneaking tricks of petty shopkeepers are thus dressed up as political maxims for governing a great empire; for it is only the pettiest shopkeepers who make it a rule to deal mainly with their own customers. A great trader always buys his goods where they are cheapest and best, with no regard for any small interest of this kind.

By maxims like these, however, nations have been taught that their interest lies in beggaring all their neighbours. Every nation has been led to look with a jealous eye on the prosperity of all the nations it trades with, and to count their gain as its own loss. Commerce, which ought naturally to be a bond of union and friendship among nations as among individuals, has become instead the most fertile source of discord and ill will. The reckless ambition of kings and ministers has not, during the present and preceding century, been more destructive of Europe's peace than the meddlesome jealousy of merchants and manufacturers. The violence and injustice of mankind's rulers is an ancient evil, for which, I fear, the nature of human affairs can scarcely admit a remedy. But the mean rapacity and monopolizing spirit of merchants and manufacturers, who neither are nor ought to be the rulers of mankind, though it perhaps cannot be cured, can very easily be kept from disturbing anyone's peace but their own.

That it was the spirit of monopoly which first invented and spread this doctrine cannot be doubted; and those who first taught it were by no means such fools as those who believed it. In every country it always is, and must be, in the interest of the great body of the people to buy whatever they want from those who sell it cheapest. The proposition is so plain that it seems ridiculous to take any trouble to prove it; nor could it ever have been questioned, had not the self-interested sophistry of merchants and manufacturers muddled the common sense of mankind. Their interest, in this respect, is directly opposed to that of the great body of the people. Just as it is in the interest of the freemen of a corporation to keep all the other inhabitants from employing any workmen but themselves, so it is in the interest of the merchants and manufacturers of every country to secure to themselves the monopoly of the home market. Hence, in Britain and most other European countries, the extraordinary duties on almost all goods imported by foreign merchants. Hence the high duties and outright bans on all foreign manufactures that could compete with our own. Hence, too, the extraordinary restraints on importing almost every sort of good from those countries with which the balance of trade is thought to run against us — that is, from those against whom national ill will happens to be most violently inflamed.

The wealth of neighbouring nations, though dangerous in war and politics, is certainly advantageous in trade. In a state of hostility it may let our enemies maintain fleets and armies stronger than our own; but in a state of peace and commerce it must also let them trade with us to a greater value, and provide a better market, whether for the immediate produce of our own industry or for whatever is bought with that produce. Just as a rich man is likely to be a better customer to the industrious people in his neighbourhood than a poor one, so too is a rich nation. A rich man who is himself a manufacturer is, indeed, a very dangerous neighbour to all who work in the same line. But all the rest of the neighbourhood — by far the greater number — profit from the good market his spending provides them. They even profit from his underselling the poorer workmen in the same line. In the same way, the manufacturers of a rich nation may no doubt be very dangerous rivals to those of their neighbours. Yet this very competition is advantageous to the great body of the people, who profit greatly besides from the good market that such a nation's large spending affords them in every other way. Private people who want to make a fortune never think of retiring to the remote, poor provinces of a country, but head for the capital or one of the great commercial towns. They know that where little wealth circulates there is little to be got, but that where a great deal is in motion some share of it may fall to them. The same maxim that would thus guide the common sense of one, or ten, or twenty individuals ought to govern the judgment of one, or ten, or twenty millions, and ought to make a whole nation regard the riches of its neighbours as a likely cause and occasion of riches for itself. A nation that means to enrich itself by foreign trade is certainly most likely to do so when its neighbours are all rich, industrious, and commercial nations. A great nation surrounded on all sides by wandering savages and poor barbarians might, no doubt, grow rich by cultivating its own lands and by its own internal commerce, but not by foreign trade. It seems to have been in this way that the ancient Egyptians and the modern Chinese acquired their great wealth. The ancient Egyptians, it is said, neglected foreign commerce, and the modern Chinese, it is well known, hold it in the utmost contempt and scarcely deign to give it the decent protection of the laws. The modern maxims of foreign commerce, by aiming at the impoverishment of all our neighbours, tend — so far as they actually achieve their intended effect — to render that very commerce trifling and contemptible.

It is because of these maxims that the commerce between France and England has, in both countries, been weighed down with so many discouragements and restraints. Yet if those two countries would only consider their real interest, free of mercantile jealousy and national ill will, the commerce of France might be more advantageous to Britain than that of any other country, and, for the same reason, that of Britain to France. France is Britain's nearest neighbour. In the trade between the southern coast of England and the northern and north-western coast of France, the returns might be expected, just as in the inland trade, four, five, or six times a year. The capital employed in this trade could therefore, in each of the two countries, keep in motion four, five, or six times the quantity of industry, and provide employment and subsistence to four, five, or six times the number of people, that an equal capital could in most other branches of foreign trade. Between the parts of France and Britain most distant from each other, the returns might be expected at least once a year; and even this trade would be at least as advantageous as most other branches of our foreign European trade. It would be at least three times more advantageous than the much-vaunted trade with our North American colonies, where the returns were seldom made in less than three years, and often not in less than four or five. France, besides, is supposed to hold 24,000,000 inhabitants. Our North American colonies were never supposed to hold more than 3,000,000; and France is a far richer country than North America, though, because riches are more unequally spread, there is much more poverty and beggary in the one than in the other. France, then, could provide a market at least eight times larger, and, given the greater frequency of returns, twenty-four times more advantageous, than our North American colonies ever did. The trade of Britain would be just as advantageous to France, and, in proportion to the wealth, population, and nearness of the two countries, would have the same superiority over the trade France carries on with her own colonies. Such is the very great difference between the trade that the wisdom of both nations has seen fit to discourage and the trade it has most favoured.

But the very same circumstances that would have made an open and free commerce between the two countries so advantageous to both have caused the chief obstructions to that commerce. Being neighbours, they are necessarily enemies, and the wealth and power of each becomes, for that reason, more alarming to the other; so that what would otherwise heighten the advantages of national friendship serves only to inflame the violence of national ill will. They are both rich and industrious nations, and the merchants and manufacturers of each dread the competition of the skill and energy of those of the other. Mercantile jealousy is roused, and both inflames and is inflamed by the violence of national ill will; and the traders of both countries have announced, with all the passionate confidence of self-interested falsehood, the certain ruin of each as a result of that unfavourable balance of trade which, they pretend, would be the inevitable effect of unrestricted commerce with the other.

There is no commercial country in Europe whose approaching ruin has not, again and again, been foretold by the supposed experts of this system as the consequence of some unfavourable balance of trade. Yet after all the alarm they have stirred up about it, and after all the futile efforts of almost every trading nation to turn that balance in its own favour and against its neighbours, it does not appear that any one nation in Europe has been impoverished by this cause in any respect. On the contrary, every town and country, as it has opened its ports to all nations, instead of being ruined by this free trade — as the principles of the commercial system would lead us to expect — has been enriched by it. Though there are a few towns in Europe that in some respects deserve the name of free ports, there is no country that does. Holland perhaps comes nearest to that character of any, though still very far from it; and Holland, it is admitted, draws not only its whole wealth but a great part of its necessary subsistence from foreign trade.

There is, indeed, another balance, already explained, very different from the balance of trade, which, as it happens to be favourable or unfavourable, necessarily brings about the prosperity or decline of every nation. This is the balance between annual produce and annual consumption. If, as already noted, the exchangeable value of the annual produce exceeds that of the annual consumption, the capital of society must increase each year in proportion to the excess. In this case society lives within its income; and what is saved each year out of that income is naturally added to its capital and employed so as to increase the annual produce still further. If, on the contrary, the exchangeable value of the annual produce falls short of the annual consumption, the capital of society must decline each year in proportion to the shortfall. In this case society's spending exceeds its income and necessarily eats into its capital. Its capital must therefore decline, and with it the exchangeable value of the annual produce of its industry.

This balance of produce and consumption is entirely different from what is called the balance of trade. It could occur in a nation that had no foreign trade at all, but was wholly cut off from the rest of the world. It could occur across the whole globe, whose wealth, population, and improvement may be either gradually increasing or gradually declining.

The balance of produce and consumption may be steadily in a nation's favour even while the so-called balance of trade generally runs against it. A nation may import more than it exports for half a century together, perhaps; the gold and silver that comes in during all this time may be sent straight out again; its circulating coin may gradually wear away, with various kinds of paper money put in its place; and even the debts it owes to the principal nations it deals with may be gradually mounting — and yet its real wealth, the exchangeable value of the annual produce of its land and labour, may, over the same period, have been increasing in a far greater proportion. The condition of our North American colonies, and of the trade they carried on with Britain before the present disturbances began {this paragraph was written in 1775}, may serve to prove that this is by no means an impossible supposition.
